## Abstract
Neuropathic pain is associated with abnormal sensations and/or pain induced by non-painful stimuli, i.e., allodynia causing burning or cold sensation, pinching of pins and needles like feeling, numbness, aching or itching. However, no suitable therapy exists to treat these pain syndromes. Our laboratory explored novel potential therapeutic strategies using a suitable composition of neurotrophic factors and active peptide fragments-Cerebrolysin (Ever Neuro Pharma, Austria) in alleviating neuropathic pain induced spinal cord pathology in a rat model. Neuropathic pain was produced by constrictions of L-5 spinal sensory nerves for 2–10 weeks period. In one group of rats cerebrolysin (2.5 or 5 ml/kg, i.v.) was administered once daily after 2 weeks until sacrifice (4, 8 and 10 weeks). Ag, Cu and Al NPs (50 mg/kg, i.p.) were delivered once daily for 1 week. Pain assessment using mechanical (Von Frey) or thermal (Hot-Plate) nociceptive showed hyperalgesia from 2 weeks until 10 weeks progressively that was exacerbated following Ag, Cu and Al NPs intoxication in nerve lesioned groups. Leakage of Evans blue and radioiodine across the blood-spinal cord barrier (BSCB) is seen from 4 to 10 weeks in the rostral and caudal cord segments associated with edema formation and cell injury. Immunohistochemistry of albumin and GFAP exhibited a close parallelism with BSCB leakage that was aggravated by NPs following nerve lesion. Light microscopy using Nissl stain exhibited profound neuronal damages in the cord. Transmission electron microcopy (TEM) show myelin vesiculation and synaptic damages in the cord that were exacerbated following NPs intoxication. Using ELISA spinal tissue exhibited increased albumin, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), myelin basic protein (MBP) and heat shock protein (HSP 72kD) upregulation together with cytokines TNF-α, IL-4, IL-6, IL-10 levels in nerve lesion that was exacerbated following NPs intoxication. Cerebrolysin treatment significantly reduced hyperalgesia and attenuated BSCB disruption, edema formation and cellular changes in nerve lesioned group. The levels of cytokines were also restored near normal levels with cerebrolysin treatment. Albumin, GFAP, MABP and HSP were also reduced in cerebrolysin treated group and thwarted neuronal damages, myelin vesiculation and cell injuries. These neuroprotective effects of cerebrolysin with higher doses were also effective in nerve lesioned rats with NPs intoxication. These observations suggest that cerebrolysin actively protects spinal cord pathology and hyperalgesia following nerve lesion and its exacerbation with metal NPs, not reported earlier.

## Introduction
Neuropathic pain causes misery and decreases quality of life in some populations the severity of that gradually enhances over time [[1]–[6]]. About 10% American and European populations suffer from neuropathic pain with more than 40% populations experience other sever pain. Spinal cord injury (SCI), multiple sclerosis (MS), ischemic stroke, uncontrolled diabetes and other metabolic diseases, herpes zoster and HIV-infections, malignancies or immune related disorders induce neuropathic like pain syndrome [[7]–[9]]. Neuropathic pain is quite prevalent in active service military population affecting their sleep, mental and physical states [[1]–[3]]. Furthermore, combat related activities and trauma to the brain and spinal cord often complicate the prevalence of neuropathic pain in service members [[4]–[6]]. The incidences of neuropathic pain may often precipitates in fatigue, anxiety, depression, social distraction and anger [[7]–[9]]. These factors affect the intelligence, decisions making ability and performances among the military populations [[10]–[14]]. Thus, the incidences of neuropathic pain require suitable care and effective treatment for leading almost normal life and active participation in the military requirements. However, so far no suitable therapeutic strategies are available to effectively treat these neuropathic pain syndromes.

Military populations are often exposed to wide variety of environmental, industrial and chemical hazards that often complicates their neuropathic pain episodes [[15]–[18]]. Thus, gun powder explosion, exposure to metal particles, sand storms, chemicals and hazardous gaseous elements affect the behavioural and functional states of these service members at battlefields or in peace keeping operations [[19]–[21]]. However, studies on external factors such as nanoparticles exposure affecting neuropathic pain induced behavioural and/or pathophysiological functions are still not well investigated.

It is quite likely that exposure of nanoparticles may affect the severity of neuropathic pain. This is evident from the findings that exposure of engineered metal nanoparticles induces blood–brain barrier (BBB) disruption and enhances morphine withdrawal induced brain pathology [[22]–[25]]. Nanoparticles exposure also adversely affects spinal cord trauma induced pathophysiology and exacerbates blood-spinal cord barrier breakdown to proteins [[26]–[28]]. In addition, engineered metal nanoparticles intoxication significantly enhanced behavioural and pathophysiological functions following heat stress at hot environments [[29]–[31]]. These studies suggest that exposure to nanoparticles may also worsen the pathophysiology of neuropathic pain.

Neuropathic pain induces upregulation of neuronal or immunologic nitric oxide synthase within the spinal cord and alters BSCB breakdown to albumin [[32]–[34]]. Alteration in the microenvironment of the spinal cord and upregulation of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) expression indicates activation of astrocytes [[32]]. The other gaseous molecule the carbon monoxide (CO) is also expressed within the spinal cord following chronic nerve lesion, a model for experimental neuropathic pain [[35]]. Treatments with inhibitors of nitric oxide synthase or antioxidants attenuate the pathophysiology of the spinal cord in neuropathic pain [[36]]. In an experimental model of spinal cord injury upregulation of the nitric oxide synthase and hemeoxygenase the enzymes responsible for nitric oxide and carbon monoxide synthesis respectively is attenuated by topical application of brain derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) or insulin like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) over the traumatized cord [[37], [38]]. These observations suggest that neurotrophic factors may be neuroprotective in neuropathic pain induced BSCB breakdown and astrocytic activation. Several reports show that glia cell derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) is equally capable to reduce spinal cord injury induced behavioural dysfunction, BSCB breakdown and structural changes within the cord tissue [[39]–[41]]. Since the pathophysiological and behavioral aspects of spinal cord injury and chronic nerve lesion indices neuropathic pain are quite similar in nature, a possibility arises that combined treatment with several key neurotrophic factors will attenuate the pathophysiology of neuropathic pain.

Keeping these views in consideration, we examined the effect of engineered metal nanoparticles Ag, Cu and Al (50–60 nm) on chronic constriction nerve injury induced neuropathic pain in the rat on behavioural, biochemical and pathophysiological aspects in our laboratory. In addition we explored the effects of a potent neuroprotective agent cerebrolysin (EverNeuroPharma, Austria)- that is a balanced composition of several neurotrophic factors and active peptide fragments for the first time in experimental neuropathic pain [[42], [43]]. Our results clearly show that metal nanoparticles exacerbate the magnitude and severity of neuropathic pain on behavioural, biochemical and pathological changes within the spinal cord and cerebrolysin could induce profound neuroprotection in these settings.

## Materials and Methods

## Animals
Experiments were carried out on 348 male albino Wistar Rats (300–350 g body wt.) housed at controlled ambient temperature (21 ± 1 ℃) with 12 h light and 12 h dark schedule (Table 1). The rat feed and tap water were supplied ad libitum. All experiments were conducted on animals with Care and Handling of animals without any pain as per the Guidelines of National Institute of Health and approved by the Local Institutional Ethics Committee [[44]].

## Chronic Constriction of Spinal Nerves
Neuropathic pain was inflicted in the rat using chronic constriction of spinal nerves as described in the literature [[34], [45], [46]]. In brief, under Halothane anesthesia, left spinal nerves at L5 and L6 was dissected out and tightly sutured with a 5.0 Silk thread (Ethicon, Cincinnati, OH, USA). After that, the wound is closed aseptically and animals were allowed to recover as described earlier [[34], [45], [46]].

In sham group, the left spinal nerves L5 and L6 were exposed identically but not ligated. The wound was sutured and post surgical care was given identically as the nerve ligated group. In some cases, intact animals also served as controls [[46]].

No spontaneous pain behavior was seen in any group of animals. Hypersensitivity to pain could be seen when provoked either by mechanical or thermal stimulation. No abnormal locomotion or gait was observed in any group examined over 10 weeks.

## Survival Periods
The control, sham group and nerve-ligated groups were allowed to survive for 4, 8 or 10 weeks after the surgery (Table 1).

## Exposure to Nanoparticles
Engineered metal nanoparticles Ag, Cu or Al (50–60 nm, Wright-Patterson, Air Force Base, Dayton, OH, USA as a Gift) were administered in Tween 80% in 09% NaCl solution in a dose of 50 mg/kg (i.p.) once daily for 1 week in individual animals (Fig. 1) [[47], [48]].

[Fig. 1: Nerve lesion protocol. Spinal nerve lesion was inflicted in the rat and all parameters are examined after 4 weeks (4 wk), 8 weeks (8 wk) or 10 weeks (10 wk) survival. Nanoparticles (NP) were administered intraperitoneally 1 week (1 wk) before nerve lesion. Cerebrolysin (CBL) was administered intravenously (i.v.) for 2 weeks 10 10 wk nerve lesion (NL) group and parameters are examined (for details see text)]

Control, sham and nerve-lesioned animals were treated identically with nanoparticles. In one group of animals only vehicle was administered daily for 1 week [[47], [48]].

## Pain Hypersensitivity Test
All animal groups were subjected to mechanical pain hypersensitivity using Von Frey method as described earlier. Also thermal pain test were done in which the animals tail is exposed to radiant heat stimulus or hot plate and the response of tail flick was recorded [[49]–[52]].

## Cerebrolysin Treatment
Cerebrolysin (EverNeuroPharma, Austria) was administered in control, sham and nerve lesioned group in a dose of 2.5 or 5 ml/kg intravenously (Fig. 1) through an indwelling polythene cannula implanted aseptically into the right femoral vein 1 week before the experiments and flushed with heparin saline daily to keep it patent [[53]–[55]].

In sham, control or nerve lesioned animals with or without nanoparticles intoxication either 2.5 ml or 5 ml/kg dose of cerebrolysin was administered once daily for 2 weeks.

## Parameters Examined
The following parameters were examined in all animal groups using standard protocol as described in the literature (see below).

## Physiological Variables
The mean arterial blood pressure (MABP), arterial pH and blood gases (PaO2 and PaCO2) were measured in each animal as described earlier [[56]]. In brief, the MABP was recorded from the right carotid artery (PE10) implanted 1 week before aseptically and advanced towards the heart and the other end of the cannula was taken out from the back skin and secured in place with Silk thread (Ethicon, Cincinnati, OH, USA). The arterial cannula was flushed every day with heparinized saline. At the time of recording the arterial cannula was connected to a Strain Gauge Pressure Transducer (Statham, P23, USA) and the MABP was recorded using chart recorder (Electromed, UK). Before connecting the arterial cannula to the transducer small amount of blood was withdrawn and kept or arterial pH and blood gases measurement using Radiometer apparatus (Copenhagen, Denmark) [[56]]. The heart rate and respiration rate was also recorded using chart recorder during the experiment [[47], [48]].

## Blood-Spinal Cord Barrier Permeability
The blood-spinal cord barrier (BSCB) was examined using leakage of Evans blue (2% of a 3 ml/kg solution in 0.9% physiological saline, pH 7.4) and radioactive iodine (131-I-Na 100 µCi/kg) administered intravenously though right femoral vein 10 min before termination of the experiment. The intravascular tracer is washed out with 0.9% cold saline and the spinal cord was dissected out and examined for the blue dye extravasation. After that the tissues were processed for colorimetric determination of Evans blue dye leakage in the cord. The radioactivity in the tissue samples was determined in a Gamma counter (Packard, USA) as described earlier. About 1 ml of whole blood was withdrawn from the left cardiac ventricle puncture before saline perfusion to determination whole blood radioactivity. Extravasation of radioactivity in the cord is calculated as percentage leakage of radioactivity over whole blood level of 131-Iodine-Na [[57]].

## Spinal Cord Edema
Spinal cord edema was measured using changes in the water content as described earlier [[57]–[59]]. The percent volume swelling (% ƒ) was calculated from differences in water content between control and nerve lesioned group [[57]].

## Morphological Analysis
For morphological changes in the spinal cord light and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was used according to the standard procedures. At the end of the experiments, the animals were perfused with 4% buffered paraformaldehyde preceded with a cold 0.9% saline rinse. After the perfusion with fixative, the spinal cord tissues were removed and processed for histological using Nissl or Haematoxylin & Eosin (H&E) and immunohistochemical study for albumin, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) at the light microscope. For TEM, the tissues were postfixed in OsO4 and embedded in Plastic (Epon 812). The ultrathin sections were cut with a diamond knife at ultramicrotome and counterstained and examined under a Phillips 400 TEM for myelin vesiculation and neuropil ultrastructural changes as described earlier [[32], [34], [58], [59]].

## Biochemical Analyses
In order to corroborate immunohistochemical studies, albumin, GFAP, myelin basic protein and HSP 72kD was measured in the spinal cord samples using Rat ELISA kits from MyBioSource (San Diego, CA, USA) according to commercial protocol. In addition, interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), IL-10 and IL-4 was also measured in spinal cord samples using commercial ELISA kits [[60]–[68]].

## Statistical Treatment of the Data Obtained
ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s test for multiple group comparison was done using one control group using commercial software StatView 5 (Abacus Concept, USA) on a Macintosh computer in Classic Environment. A p-value less than 0.05 was considered significant.

## Physiological Variables
Changes in the body weight, rectal temperature, heart rate and respiration rate were examined in control, sham and nerve lesioned rats with or without nanoparticles intoxication. The arterial pH, blood gases and mean arterial blood pressure (MABP) were examined in all groups. The results are shown in Table 2.

The body weight in nerve lesioned animals increased significantly after 4 weeks in a progressive manner and this effect was also seen following nanoparticles intoxications and cerebrolysin treatments in all groups (Table 2).

However, rectal temperature showed a slight decrease from the control or sham group following nerve lesion with or without nanoparticles treatments. On the other hand, cerebrolysin treatment attenuated this decrease in nerve lesion and nanoparticles intoxication (Table 2).

Chronic nerve lesion significantly increased heart rate as compared to controls or sham group. This increase in heart rate after nerve lesion is further potentiated with nanoparticles intoxication (Table 2). Treatment with cerebrolysin attenuated this increase in heart rate in nerve lesion with and without nanoparticles intoxication (Table 2).

Respiration rate after nerve lesion in saline treated rats showed significant decrease after 10 weeks whereas, nanoparticles intoxication significantly raised the respiration rate during 8–10 weeks of nerve lesion (Table 2)- Cerebrolysin treatment significantly attenuated this increase in respiration rate in nanoparticles intoxicated nerve lesioned arts in Ag and Cu group. However, Al nanoparticles showed significant increase in cerebrolysin treated nerve lesioned group (Table 2).

The MABP increased significantly in nerve lesioned rats progressively and this effect was further enhanced with nanoparticles intoxication and cerebrolysin treatment significantly attenuated this rise in MABP (Table 2). The arterial pH exhibited slight decrease in nerve lesioned group with or without nanoparticles intoxication; however, the values were not significantly altered (Table 2). The PaO2 significantly increased after nerve lesion that was exacerbated in Ag and Cu nanoparticles administered group except in Al nanoparticles exposed rats after nerve lesion (Table 2). Cerebrolysin treatment markedly thwarts this rise in PaO2 following nerve lesion with or without exposure (Table 2). On the other hand, PaCO2 significantly elevated after nerve lesion and further exacerbated with nanoparticles exposure in nerve lesion group. Cerebrolysin treatment significantly attenuated this increase in PaCO2 in nerve lesion with or without nanoparticles intoxication (Table 2).

## Pain Hypersensitivity
Control and sham treated animals with or without nanoparticles treatment did not show hypersensitivity to mechanical or thermal stimulations.

Pain hypersensitivity was measured in nerve lesioned group with or without nanoparticles exposure using mechanical stimulation or thermal stimulation. Von Frey hair stimulation weight and latency of paw withdrawal significantly reduced in nerve lesioned rats progressively with time (Table 3). This effect was further exacerbated with nanoparticles exposure. Treatment with cerebrolysin significantly enhanced the weight of Von Frey hair with almost identical paw withdrawal latency in nerve lesioned group with or without nanoparticles intoxication (Table 3).

Likewise thermal radiant stimulus induced tail flick latency showed significant reduction in nerve lesioned group with or without nanoparticles exposure. However, cerebrolysin treatment significantly enhanced the tail flick latency following thermal stimulus in nerve lesioned rats with or without nanoparticles intoxication (Table 3).

## Blood-Spinal Cord Barrier Breakdown
Breakdown of the BSCB was measured using leakage of Evans blue albumin (EBA) and radioactive iodine in nerve lesioned rats with or without nanoparticles intoxication. The results are shown in Table 4. Nerve lesioned rats exhibited significant leakage of EBA and 131-I within the spinal cord segments T10-11 and L5-S2 progressively from 4 to 10 weeks of nerve lesion (Table 3). This breakdown of the BSCB to EBA and radioiodine was further exacerbated following nanoparticles exposure (Table 4). Treatment with cerebrolysin significantly attenuated the BSCB leakage of EBA or radioiodine in these segments after nerve lesion with or without nanoparticles exposure (Table 4).

## Spinal Cord Edema Formation and Volume Swelling
Leakage of serum proteins into the spinal cord induces edema formation and volume swelling. Thus, edema formation was measured using spinal cord water content and volume swelling (%ƒ) was calculated from the changes of water content as described earlier.

The results are shown in Table 4. Spinal nerve lesion significantly caused edema formation and volume swelling within the cord that was progressive over 4–10 weeks of nerve lesion. This effect was further enhanced with nanoparticles exposure (Table 4).

Treatment with cerebrolysin significantly attenuated edema formation and volume swelling in nerve lesioned group with or without nanoparticles exposure (Table 4).

## Biochemical Changes
We previously reported increased albumin and GFAP immunohistochemistry following chronic nerve lesion from 4 to 10 weeks that showed maximum increase at 10 weeks of nerve lesion. In this study, we measured albumin, GFAP, myelin basic protein (MBP) and heat shock protein 72 kD (HSP 72 kD) using ELISA. The results are shown in Table 5.

Nerve lesion significantly enhanced albumin levels in the spinal cord progressively from 4 to 10 weeks following the lesion. Intoxication of nanoparticles further enhanced the albumin levels within the spinal cord. Treatment with cerebrolysin significantly thwarted this increase in albumin level in the spinal cord segments after nerve lesion (Table 5).

On the other hand, GFAP Elisa exhibited also significant rise in the spinal cord of nerve lesioned group from 4th to 10th week progressively (Table 5). This was further exacerbated following nanoparticles intoxication in nerve lesioned groups (Table 5). However, cerebrolysin treatment significantly reduced GFAP levels within the spinal cord segments in both nanoparticles exposed group and normal nerve lesion rats (Table 5).

Measurement of MBP levels showed significant increase within the spinal cord as compared from the control or sham operated animals following nerve lesion. This increase in MBP denoting breakdown of myelin was seen 4 weeks after the nerve lesion that progressively increased throughout up to 10 weeks period (Table 5). Exposure of nanoparticles further exacerbated MBP levels within the spinal cord after nerve lesion. Interestingly, cerebrolysin treatment significantly attenuated myelin degradation after nerve lesion with or without nanoparticle exposure as is evident from reduction in MBP levels within the cord (Table 5).

Likewise the stress of chronic nerve lesion significantly enhanced HSP 72 kD protein levels within the spinal cord segments progressively from 4 weeks period to 10 weeks duration. Intoxication with nanoparticle exacerbated HSP 72 kD levels in the spinal cord segments after nerve lesion in animals (Table 5).

Treatment with cerebrolysin in nerve lesioned group either with nanoparticles exposure or without them significantly reduced the HSP 72 kD levels within the spinal cord (Table 5).

## Measurement of Cytokines in Nerve Lesion
The levels of both inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines were measured within the spinal cord of control, sham and nerve lesioned group with or without nanoparticles exposure. The levels of TNF-α and IL-6 as inflammatory cytokines and IL-10 and IL-4 as anti-inflammatory cytokines are displayed in Table 6.

The results show that both inflammatory cytokine significantly increased within the spinal cord segments after nerve lesion from 4th to 10th week of survival in a progressive manner (Table 6). Intoxication with nanoparticle further enhanced the inflammatory cytokine after nerve lesion within the spinal cord segments significantly (Table 6).

The anti-inflammatory cytokine also enhanced after nerve lesion from 4th to 8th week but declined at 10th week of survival. On the other hand, nanoparticles exposure in nerve lesion resulted in further exacerbation from 4th to 10th week after nerve lesion in a progressive manner (Table 6).

Treatment with cerebrolysin significantly reduced the accumulation of inflammatory cytokines in the spinal cord after 10th week of nerve lesion. This effect was also seen in nerve lesioned group intoxicated with nanoparticles significantly with cerebrolysin (Table 6). Whereas cerebrolysin was able to enhance anti-inflammatory cytokines in the spinal cord significantly at 10th week after nerve lesioned group either with or without nanoparticles exposure (Table 6).

## Spinal Cord Morphology
Spinal cord morphology was examined using standard histopathological techniques and immunocytochemistry in nerve lesioned group intoxicated with nanoparticles. Semiquantitative analysis of data was also done on the spinal cord segments at T10, T12 and L5 in all groups.

## Neuronal Injury
Analysis of neuronal injury in Nissl or H&E stained 3-µm thick paraffin sections were counted for neuronal distortion, dark neurons or chromatolysis and counted in each segment by 3 independent observes. The median values were taken in account in 6 to 8 different animals and shown in Fig. 2. As seen within the graph the numbers of neuronal injury following nerve lesion in the T10, T12 and L5 segments is significantly increased as compared to the control group. This increase in neural injury is further exacerbated following Cu or Ag nanoparticles with nerve lesion (Fig. 2). There was a significant increase in neuronal injury after nerve lesion with or without nanoparticles after 8 and 10 weeks as compared to the 4 weeks lesion from the control group of different spinal cord segments (Fig. 2).

headline.statement: Five significance decisions in the paper's two behavioural/physiological tables contradict the group means and standard deviations printed beside them: four asterisked cells cannot reach p < 0.05 under any standard test, and one comparison the text calls "not significantly altered" has a p-value below 0.002.
headline.evidence: Table 2, Respiration cycle/min: Control "14 ± 3"; Nerve Lesion 4 wk "12 ± 9*"; Nerve Lesion 10 wk "12 ± 8*"; §CBL + NL + Al 10 wk "16 ± 6*". Table 3, Paw Withdrawal Latency (Sec): Control "6 ± 3"; NL + Al NPs 10 wk "4 ± 5*". Footnotes define "*P < 0.05 ... from control group" and "Values are Mean ± SD of 6–8 rats at each point." Taking n = 8 per group (the top of the paper's own stated range, the assumption most favourable to the authors) and allowing every rounding of the printed integers, the achievable two-tailed p-intervals are [0.354, 0.786], [0.301, 0.765], [0.182, 0.709] and [0.122, 0.672] respectively; the one-tailed intervals are [0.177, 0.393], [0.151, 0.383], [0.091, 0.355] and [0.061, 0.336]. Conversely Table 2, Arterial pH: Control "7.38 ± 0.04" versus NL + Ag NPs 10 wk "7.23 ± 0.06" (no asterisk), against the Results sentence "the values were not significantly altered (Table 2)"; at n = 6 per group the entire achievable p-interval is [0.00013, 0.00194].
headline.plain: The paper marks certain measurements with a star to say they differ significantly from the untreated control animals. For four of those starred results, the averages and spreads printed in the same row are simply too close together for any standard statistical test to declare a difference -- no matter which of the permitted group sizes or rounding you assume. Separately, one comparison the authors describe in words as showing no significant difference is in fact a large, clearly significant difference by the same arithmetic. The errors run in both directions, which means the pattern of stars in these tables cannot be reproduced from the paper's own data.

findings.computed: At n = 8 per group and allowing every rounding of the printed 0-decimal means and SDs, the achievable two-tailed p-intervals are [0.354, 0.786], [0.301, 0.765], [0.182, 0.709] and [0.122, 0.672]; one-tailed [0.177, 0.393], [0.151, 0.383], [0.091, 0.355] and [0.061, 0.336]. p = 0.05 lies outside every interval under Welch's and Student's tests, one- and two-tailed. All four returned severity `highly_suspicious` with the verdict "Reported p bound = 0.05 is UNREACHABLE".
findings.assumptions: n = 8 per group, the TOP of the paper's own stated range "6–8 rats at each point" and the value most favourable to the authors' significance claim; at n = 6 every p would be larger still. The rounding intervals follow from the paper's own footnote that "the values are adjusted to nearest numbers". The paper states its analysis was ANOVA followed by Dunnett's test, which is more conservative than the unadjusted t-tests recomputed here, so the discrepancy can only widen under the authors' own method. No external bound was supplied.

consequence.explanation: One of the four is a primary pain outcome underpinning the abstract's hyperalgesia claim (paw-withdrawal latency worsened by aluminium nanoparticles at 10 weeks), one is a cerebrolysin-treatment claim ("Al nanoparticles showed significant increase in cerebrolysin treated nerve lesioned group"), and one supports the Results sentence "Respiration rate after nerve lesion in saline treated rats showed significant decrease after 10 weeks".

findings.plain: Four results are flagged in the tables as statistically significant differences from the untreated animals. When you take the averages and the spread of values the authors themselves printed in those same rows, and give them every benefit of the doubt about group size and rounding, no standard test can produce a significant result -- the calculated likelihood of chance is between roughly 12% and 79%, where under 5% is required. One of these is a headline pain measurement the paper's main conclusion rests on, and another is a claimed benefit of the drug being tested.

findings.title: Arterial pH difference declared non-significant in the Results while its own printed values imply p below 0.002
findings.location: Results, Physiological Variables paragraph, against Table 2 Arterial pH (Control vs NL + Ag NPs 10 wk)
findings.reported: "The arterial pH exhibited slight decrease in nerve lesioned group with or without nanoparticles intoxication; however, the values were not significantly altered (Table 2)." Table 2 prints Control 7.38 ± 0.04 and NL + Ag NPs 10 wk 7.23 ± 0.06, with no significance marker on the latter.
findings.computed: At n = 6 per group the recomputed t is 5.10 at the printed values, with the whole achievable interval running t ∈ [4.34, 6.01] and p ∈ [0.00013, 0.00194] across every admissible rounding, under both Welch's and Student's tests. The entire interval lies below 0.002 -- roughly 25-fold below the paper's own alpha of 0.05.
findings.assumptions: n = 6 per group, the BOTTOM of the stated "6–8 rats" range and the value most favourable to the authors' claim of no difference; at n = 8 the p-values would be smaller still. Rounding intervals taken from the printed 2-decimal precision. Note the direction of triage: the tool's own aggregate label for this call was `suspicious`, awarded on its heuristic that the t-interval is wide and the exact statistic cannot be pinned down; that heuristic is about precision, not about the non-significance claim. The substantive point is separate and is read off the same tool output -- the whole achievable interval sits below the paper's alpha -- so this finding is recorded one band higher than the tool's own label, and the reason is stated here rather than hidden.

consequence.explanation: The Results sentence stating arterial pH was "not significantly altered" is contradicted by Table 2's own means and SDs; a fall from pH 7.38 to 7.23 is a marked acidosis reported by the paper as absent.

findings.plain: The paper says in words that blood acidity did not change meaningfully in any group. But the numbers it prints in its own table show the nerve-injured animals given silver nanoparticles at 10 weeks had a blood pH of 7.23 against 7.38 in controls -- a difference so large relative to the spread of values that the chance of it arising randomly is under one in five hundred, at the group size most favourable to the authors' claim. This is a real and clinically meaningful shift toward acid blood that the paper reports as no change.

findings.title: Three mutually irreconcilable animal totals in Table 1: 348 stated, 362 in the cells, 368 in the row totals
findings.location: Table 1 (Experimental Protocol in Nerve Lesion), Materials and Methods; and the Animals section
findings.reported: "Experiments were carried out on 348 male albino Wistar Rats". Table 1's printed Grand Total row reads 106 / 112 / 130 / 348. Three per-group row totals read 22, 22 and 24 against cells of 6+6+8, 6+6+8 and 8+6+8.
findings.computed: Exact integer arithmetic at tolerance 0: 6 of 7 checked sums fail. Three row totals over-state their own cells by exactly 2 each (printed 22 vs 20; 22 vs 20; 24 vs 22). Two column Grand Totals under-state the cells above them -- the Physiological/Pain/Morphological column sums to 114 against a printed 106 (difference 8), and BSCB & Edema sums to 118 against a printed 112 (difference 6). The Biochemical Analyses column reconciles exactly at 130. The 18 printed per-group Total values sum to 368 against the stated 348 (difference 20), while the individual cells sum to 362. The printed grand total of 348 is arithmetically consistent only with the three (incorrect) column totals, not with the animals actually listed.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. Animal counts must hold exactly, so the tolerance was set to zero rather than to a rounding window; every input is an integer read directly from the table. The row errors are all +2 in the same direction, which is more consistent with a transcription or typesetting slip than with a random arithmetic error -- but it is the sample size of the whole study, and no printed figure reconciles with any other.

consequence.explanation: The number of animals contributing to the physiological/pain tables and to the barrier tables is stated two ways differing by 8 and 6 respectively, and the per-group n that every significance test in Tables 2-6 depends on cannot be pinned down for three groups.

findings.plain: The paper says 348 rats were used. Its own allocation table gives two other answers: adding up the individual entries gives 362 animals, and adding up the table's own per-group subtotals gives 368. Three group subtotals are each two animals larger than the entries they are supposed to add up, and two column totals are 8 and 6 animals smaller than the entries above them. These are whole animals, so there is no rounding that could explain the gaps -- at least some of the printed figures must be wrong, and the study's headline sample size cannot be recovered from the table meant to define it.

findings.title: Descriptive statistics deliberately rounded to whole numbers, leaving most significance claims unadjudicable
findings.location: Footnotes to Tables 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6; Table 2 (Body wt, Respiration) and Table 3 (Von Frey, Paw Withdrawal) cells
findings.reported: Every results-table footnote states: "Values are Mean ± SD of 6–8 rats at each point. For simplicity, the values are adjusted to nearest numbers." Consequently Table 2 prints respiration as "14 ± 3", "16 ± 3*", and Table 3 prints paw withdrawal latency as "6 ± 3", "4 ± 3*".
findings.computed: For Table 2's §CBL+NL+Al 8 wk respiration (16 ± 3* vs 14 ± 3) and Table 3's §CBL+NL+Ag 10 wk paw withdrawal (4 ± 3* vs 6 ± 3), the achievable two-tailed p-interval across the rounding box is [0.031, 0.577] with a point value of 0.204 -- reachable but not pinned, so the asterisk is neither confirmed nor refuted. For Table 2's #CBL + NL 10 wk body weight (274 ± 8* vs 267 ± 8) the smallest achievable two-tailed p is 0.051, so that asterisk is reachable only under a one-tailed test the paper never states it used, and only at the extreme corner of the rounding box at n = 8. Running the whole of Table 3 through the table dispatcher typed all 54 cells correctly as mean ± SD and then ran zero checks on them: 0 of 54, because the outcomes are continuous and no cell carries its own n.
findings.assumptions: n = 8 per group where a significance claim was tested. The rounding intervals follow directly from the paper's own statement that values were adjusted to the nearest whole number; no bound was invented. Rounding to integers is a legitimate presentational choice and is not itself an error -- the consequence, not the practice, is what is reported here.

consequence.explanation: Six further asterisked comparisons in Tables 2 and 3 can be neither confirmed nor refuted from the printed precision, so the pain and cerebrolysin claims resting on them are unverifiable rather than demonstrably wrong.

findings.plain: The authors state they rounded all their averages and spreads to whole numbers "for simplicity". A whole-number average of 4 could be anything from 3.5 to 4.5, and that uncertainty is large enough that for six further starred results the underlying test could plausibly have come out either significant or not -- there is no way to tell from what is printed. One claimed effect on body weight only reaches significance if an unstated one-sided test was used at the largest permitted group size. None of these is evidence of an error; they are results the paper does not give a reader enough information to check.

findings.title: Twenty-six animals allocated to biochemical analysis in the aluminium groups, with no aluminium data in either biochemical table
findings.location: Table 1 (rows F. Nerve Lesion+Al-NPs 4/8/10 wk and G. Nerve Lesion + Al-NPs 5 ml, Biochemical Analyses column) against Tables 5 and 6
findings.reported: Table 1's Biochemical Analyses column allocates 6, 6, 6 and 8 animals to the four aluminium-nanoparticle groups. Tables 5 and 6 contain only Control, Sham, Nerve Lesion, #CBL + NL, NL + Ag NPs, §CBL + NL + Ag, NL + Cu NPs and §CBL + NL + Cu rows; both captions read "...intoxication with Ag and Cu nanoparticle...". The abstract nonetheless states that ELISA showed albumin, GFAP, MBP, HSP 72kD and the four cytokines were elevated "in nerve lesion that was exacerbated following NPs intoxication", having named Ag, Cu and Al as the nanoparticles studied.
findings.computed: Summation of the four Al-group Biochemical Analyses allocations: 6 + 6 + 6 + 8 = 26 animals, consistent (tolerance 0). No aluminium row exists anywhere in Table 5 (20 rows) or Table 6 (20 rows), so none of those 26 animals contributes a reported biochemical value.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The reading rests on Table 1's own column heading ("Biochemical Analyses") matching the content of Tables 5 and 6 (ELISA protein and cytokine measurements), which is how the Methods describe the biochemical stream. It is possible the aluminium biochemistry was run and simply not reported, or that the Table 1 allocation is aspirational; either explanation is ordinary, and the point is that the paper does not say which.

consequence.explanation: The abstract's biochemical claim is stated for nanoparticle intoxication generally after naming all three metals, but only silver and copper were measured, so the aluminium part of that claim has no supporting data in the paper.

findings.plain: The study's own protocol table sets aside 26 rats for laboratory protein and inflammation measurements in the aluminium-nanoparticle groups. Neither of the two tables reporting those measurements contains an aluminium group at all. The summary at the front of the paper describes these biochemical effects as being worsened by nanoparticles after listing all three metals, but only silver and copper were actually measured, so no data in the paper supports that part of the statement for aluminium.

findings.title: Five unreadable numerals and a corrupted sample-size footnote in the published barrier and biochemical tables
findings.location: Table 4 ([131]-Iodine and Water content columns) and Table 5 (Albumin and HSP columns, and the Table 5 footnote)
findings.reported: Table 4: "2–16 ± 0.42**" (NL+Ag 8 wk, iodine T10-11); "1.84´0.33**" (NL+Al 10 wk, iodine T10-11); "65.63´0.34*#" (CBL+NL+Al 10 wk, water content L5-S2). Table 5: "3.28 ± 1–14**" (NL+Ag 8 wk, albumin L5-S2); "24.59´2.08**" (NL+Ag 4 wk, HSP L5-S2). Table 5 footnote: "Values are Mean ± SD of–8 rats at each point."
findings.computed: Five data cells and one footnote are malformed in the version of record. Two cells print an en-dash where a decimal point belongs ("2–16" for what must be 2.16; "1–14" for 1.14) and three print an acute accent where the ± belongs. The Table 5 footnote has lost the "6" that the other four table footnotes print, leaving the sample size of that whole table undefined. I re-read Table 5's cells and footnote directly from the publisher XML and confirmed all three defects there; Stage 1 additionally reconciled the XML against PDF pages 7 and 8 and found the two sources agree exactly on all six, so these are defects in the published article and not artefacts of extraction.
findings.assumptions: None. The reconstruction of "2–16" as 2.16 and "1–14" as 1.14 is inference from the surrounding column values and is offered as the likely intent, not as an established value; the point of the finding is that the printed characters cannot be read as numbers at all. Two of the five affected cells are SD values, so no dispersion-based check can be run on them.

consequence.explanation: Five reported measurements behind starred comparisons in the barrier and biochemical tables cannot be read as numbers by any reader or re-analyst, and Table 5's footnote no longer states how many animals its values came from.

findings.plain: Five numbers in the published tables are printed with the wrong character in the middle -- a dash where the decimal point should be, or an accent mark where the plus-or-minus sign should be -- so they cannot be read as numbers at all. A footnote that should say the values come from "6-8 rats" has lost the 6, so that table no longer states its own group sizes. These same errors appear in both the publisher's structured text and its PDF, so they are in the published article rather than introduced by our reading of it.

findings.title: Control and sham tail-flick latencies of 60 and 64 seconds to a 52 °C radiant heat stimulus
findings.location: Table 3, "Radiant heat thermal stimulation of tail — Tail Latency (Sec) 52 °C", Control and Sham rows
findings.reported: Control "60 ± 3"; Sham "64 ± 2"; Nerve Lesion 10 wk "4 ± 3*"; NL + Ag NPs 10 wk "2 ± 3*". Caption specifies a "thermal radiant heat stimulus (52 °C)".
findings.computed: No forensic arithmetic applies; this is a domain-plausibility observation and is recorded as such rather than dressed up as a computation. Normal rat tail-flick latency to a radiant stimulus of roughly 52 °C is a few seconds, and cut-off times of about 10-15 seconds are conventional precisely to prevent tissue injury. A 60-64 second latency would mean uninjured animals held their tails in a noxious stimulus for a full minute. The internal contrast is also extreme: nerve-lesioned animals in the same column reach 2-4 seconds, a 15- to 30-fold range that such an assay does not normally span.
findings.assumptions: ASSUMPTION-DEPENDENT and named as such. The paper states no cut-off time, so this rests on an external benchmark not given in the paper: conventional rat tail-flick baselines and cut-offs from the thermal nociception literature. Under rulebook rule 4 an assumption-dependent finding is capped at `suspicious`, cannot be the headline, and no impossibility is claimed. A units or transcription error (for example deciseconds printed as seconds, or a different stimulus intensity than the one stated) would explain the values benignly and is the likeliest cause.

consequence.explanation: If the control tail-flick latencies are mis-scaled or mis-transcribed, the size of the thermal hyperalgesia effect the abstract reports is not interpretable in the stated units, though the direction of the effect is unaffected.

findings.plain: In the heat-sensitivity test, healthy control animals are recorded as taking 60 seconds -- and sham-operated animals 64 seconds -- to flick their tail away from a hot stimulus. In this standard test, normal animals respond within a few seconds, and researchers usually stop the test after 10 to 15 seconds specifically to avoid burning the animal. Injured animals in the same column respond in 2 to 4 seconds. The most likely explanation is a units or transcription error rather than anything about the underlying experiment, but as printed the numbers do not describe the test the paper says it ran. Note this judgement uses an outside benchmark: the paper itself never states a cut-off time.

findings.title: Figure 8 legend, the only description of the GFAP result, states the panel shows albumin leakage
findings.reported: "Upper panel: Graphic representation of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) positive immunoreactive cells... Treatment with nanoparticles (NPs) Cu or Ag (50–60 nm) exacerbated albumin leakage at 4, 8 or 10 weeks from the nerve lesioned group significantly." The same caption prints "CBK 5 ml/kg, i.v." for CBL.
findings.computed: The sentence describing the plotted effect is the wording of the Figure 5 legend, which really is the albumin figure. Figure 8 is defined by its own caption as GFAP immunoreactivity, and that caption is the only place the plotted quantities are described -- the values appear in no table and nowhere in the body text.
findings.assumptions: None beyond comparison of the Figure 5 and Figure 8 captions as printed. This is duplicated boilerplate, the most ordinary of copy-editing errors, and no arithmetic claim is made. Its weight comes only from the fact that the legend is load-bearing: nothing else in the paper says what Figure 8 plots.

consequence.explanation: The only description of what Figure 8 plots names the wrong protein, so the GFAP cell-count result cannot be interpreted with confidence from the paper as published.

findings.plain: Figure 8 is supposed to show counts of cells stained for one particular brain protein. Its caption opens by saying so, then describes the effect being plotted as leakage of a completely different protein -- wording copied from the caption of an earlier figure. Because the caption is the only place in the paper that explains what this figure measures, a reader cannot be sure which of the two proteins the graph actually shows.

findings.title: Identical mean and standard deviation for rectal temperature and arterial CO2 in the same Table 2 row
findings.location: Table 2, NL + Cu NPs 10 wk row: Rectal T °C and PaCO2 Torr cells
findings.reported: Rectal T °C "36.89 ± 0.54"; PaCO2 Torr "36.89 ± 0.54*" -- a body temperature in degrees Celsius and an arterial carbon dioxide tension in Torr, matching to two decimals on both the mean and the spread.
findings.computed: Comparing the rectal temperature and PaCO2 columns as two 18-cell blocks yields 306 pairwise comparisons and exactly one identical (mean, SD) pair, at a corrected coincidence probability of 0.034. This is materially weaker than the 0.00011 the Stage-1 sweep reported: that figure came from a span model fitted to all eight physiological variables at once, which understates how much these two particular columns overlap. Re-running the check scoped to only the two columns that actually share the 35-37 numeric range is the honest test, and it is the number quoted here.
findings.assumptions: The two cells describe the same animals (the same table row), so this is not a case of independent samples matching; it is two different physical quantities on one group of rats. The value is not round, so the round-number discount does not apply. A coincidence probability of 0.034 for one pair among 306 comparisons is a weak signal, and coincidence remains a plausible explanation alongside a typesetting or copy-paste slip. Per rulebook rule 11 this is capped at `suspicious`; duplication is improbable, never impossible.

consequence.explanation: Neither value carries a claim in the paper's argument; the relevance is to the provenance of the Table 2 numbers generally, not to any conclusion.

findings.plain: In one row of the physiology table, the animals' body temperature and their blood carbon dioxide level are printed with exactly the same average and exactly the same spread, to two decimal places -- despite being entirely different things measured in different units. These two quantities happen to fall in a similar numeric range, so this can happen by chance; our estimate is roughly a 3% chance across all the comparisons available in that table. It is worth a query about how the table was assembled, not a conclusion about the study.

findings.title: Several hundred group-versus-control comparisons reported only as asterisks, with no test statistic, degrees of freedom or exact p anywhere
findings.location: Statistical Treatment section; Tables 2-6; Figures 2, 5 and 8
findings.reported: "ANOVA followed by Dunnett's test for multiple group comparison was done using one control group using commercial software StatView 5 (Abacus Concept, USA)... A p-value less than 0.05 was considered significant." Every result is carried by "*P < 0.05; **P < 0.01 from control group, #P < 0.05 from Nerve lesion".
findings.computed: An automated NHST extraction over all 25 PDF pages recovered zero test statistics: the paper contains no F, no t, no degrees of freedom and no exact p-value anywhere. Multiplicity arithmetic could not be run either -- all 51 Table 3 comparisons submitted were dropped because their p-values are thresholds rather than values, leaving 0 evaluable tests, so no family-wise error rate and no count of claims lost to correction can be computed. The scale, from the sweep's own enumeration of the table dimensions, is on the order of 500 group-versus-control comparisons against a single shared control (Table 2: 8 variables × 17 groups; Table 3: 3 × 17; Table 4: 6 × 17; Tables 5 and 6: 8 × 14 each), plus three figure panels. The stated Dunnett's adjustment operates only within a single measure's ANOVA -- it does not span the eight variables of Table 2, the three measures of Table 3, or the five tables.
findings.assumptions: None. `indeterminate` here is a refusal, not a pass: nothing could be verified by direct recalculation, which is why every check in this review had to go the longer route of reconstructing tests from the group descriptives. The multiplicity tool's refusal to coerce thresholded p-values is deliberate and is the correct behaviour; the consequence is simply that the question cannot be answered from what is printed.

consequence.explanation: Every inferential claim in the paper is unauditable by direct recalculation, and how many of roughly 500 asterisked comparisons would survive correction across measures cannot be determined from what is printed.

findings.plain: Statistics papers normally print the numbers behind each test so a reader can check them. This paper prints none -- no test values, no measures of sample structure, no exact probabilities. Every one of roughly five hundred comparisons is communicated by a star next to a number. That makes direct checking impossible; everything in this review had to be worked backwards from the averages instead. It also means there is no way to tell how many of those five hundred results would still count as significant once you account for the sheer number of comparisons being made against the same control group.

findings.title: Data availability statement directing enquiries to the authors, with no deposited data or supplementary files
findings.location: Data Availability and Data Availability Statement sections
findings.reported: "Enquiries about data availability should be directed to the authors." Funders listed include the Air Force Office of Scientific Research, NIH R01 AG028679, the Swedish Medical Research Council and EverNeuroPharma.
findings.computed: No repository, accession number or supplementary data file is named for a 348-animal study supported by multiple public funders and by the manufacturer of the tested compound. No supplementary materials of any kind accompany the article, so no participant-level duplication analysis could be attempted.
findings.assumptions: None. This is a weak signal on its own and is recorded as such; directing enquiries to authors was a common and accepted convention. Its relevance here is specific: the per-animal values would settle the Table 1 accounting and every unreachable-p asterisk at once, and they are the one thing that could.

consequence.explanation: None of the numeric discrepancies identified in this review can be resolved by a reader, because the underlying data are not available.

findings.plain: The paper does not make its data available; it says to ask the authors. That is an accepted convention and not by itself a problem. It matters here only because the underlying animal-by-animal measurements are exactly what would settle every discrepancy described above, and they are not obtainable from the published article.

findings.title: Retracted status of the version of record, with the retraction notice not among the supplied files
findings.location: Article title in the version of record (JATS XML article-meta and PDF)
findings.reported: "RETRACTED ARTICLE: Cerebrolysin Attenuates Exacerbation of Neuropathic Pain, Blood-spinal Cord Barrier Breakdown and Cord Pathology Following Chronic Intoxication of Engineered Ag, Cu or Al (50–60 nm) Nanoparticles"
findings.computed: Contextual metadata, not a forensic result. The publisher's stated grounds for retraction are unknown to this review; the notice itself was not among the supplied files.
findings.assumptions: None. Nothing in this review reconstructs, endorses or is derived from the publisher's grounds. Every finding above was computed independently from the paper's own printed numbers and stands or falls on its own; the retraction is recorded because it bears on how the paper should be cited, not because it evidences anything checked here.

consequence.explanation: Bears on how the paper's claims should be cited, but does not itself establish anything about the numbers checked here.

findings.plain: The published version of this article carries the word RETRACTED in its title, meaning the journal has withdrawn it. The notice explaining why was not provided to us, so we do not know the publisher's reasons, and nothing in this review is based on them. Everything above was worked out from the article's own numbers.

not_checked.location: Figures 2, 5 and 8 (neuronal injury counts, albumin-positive cell counts, GFAP-positive cell counts)
not_checked.reason: These three figures carry group means, SDs and significance markers for 6-8 rats per point that appear nowhere in the text or in any table. They are the sole source for the neuronal-injury, albumin-immunoreactivity and GFAP-immunoreactivity results, and each supports a claim made in the abstract. Figure extraction was not run and no values were digitised. Anything read off these plots would carry figure-pixel provenance and would in any case be barred from the granularity checks. This is a real hole in coverage, not a formality: a substantial block of the paper's inferential claims was not examined at all.

not_checked.location: Remaining starred comparisons in Tables 2, 4, 5 and 6 (on the order of 450 cells)
not_checked.reason: Twelve comparisons were reconstructed individually, chosen as those with the smallest mean differences relative to their SDs -- i.e. where a significance claim was most likely to be unsupportable. The rest were not recalculated. The four unreachable-p results should be read as a FLOOR on the number of unsupportable asterisks in this paper, established by a targeted rather than exhaustive search, not as a count of them.

not_checked.location: Table 4, Volume Swelling (%f) columns (T10-11 and L5-S2), all rows
not_checked.reason: Volume swelling is derived: "volume swelling (%ƒ) was calculated from the changes of water content as described earlier". The paper cites a prior method but never states the transformation, so the mapping from the water-content column to the swelling column is not reproducible from anything printed here. Checking it would require assuming a conversion factor the paper does not give. The column also carries no SDs and no significance markers.

not_checked.location: Tables 2, 4, 5 and 6 -- per-cell granularity checks (GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE, DEBIT)
not_checked.reason: Correctly inapplicable and not run. Every variable in these tables is a continuous physiological or biochemical measure, which bars the integer-data granularity family outright; applying it would manufacture impossibilities out of ordinary measurements. Every footnote also states n only as a range ("6-8 rats at each point"), which bars the dispersion checks too. The dispatcher run on Table 3 is the representative denominator: all 54 cells typed correctly as mean ± SD, and 0 of 54 checks could run.

not_checked.location: Exact per-cell sample sizes throughout Tables 2-6 and Figures 2, 5, 8
not_checked.reason: The paper states n only as "6-8 rats at each point", and Table 5's footnote is corrupted to "of–8 rats". No cell carries its own n. Every significance recalculation therefore had to assume a value: n = 8 where the aim was to test a significance claim and n = 6 where the aim was to test a non-significance claim, in each case the assumption most favourable to the authors.

not_checked.location: Table 2 -- reconciliation against the publisher PDF
not_checked.reason: Stage 1 reconciled Tables 3, 4 and 5 against PDF pages 6-8 and found exact agreement with the XML, including on the corrupted cells; Table 2 was not put through that cross-check. Three of the four unreachable-p findings come from Table 2. The XML table carried no alignment warnings and its 144 cells are internally coherent, and the Table 3 finding (which was PDF-reconciled) stands independently, but the gap is recorded.

Deliberately not run, and this is the right call rather than an omission. These methods test whether randomised arms are more similar at baseline than allocation allows. This is a non-randomised laboratory experiment with deliberately constructed treatment groups and no baseline table of randomised arms, so the null those tests assume does not exist here and any verdict would be meaningless. Rulebook rule 1 (uniformly high baseline p-values as a red flag) has nothing to attach to in this paper.

Deliberately not run. The paper attributes every comparison to ANOVA with Dunnett's test; no Mann-Whitney or Wilcoxon rank-sum test is reported anywhere. Applying GRIM-U to ANOVA p-values is the toolkit's single most likely route to a false accusation, and the gate is the analyst's, not the tool's.

not_checked.location: Duplication scanning of Tables 3, 4, 5 and 6 against each other and against Table 2
not_checked.reason: Only Table 2 was scanned. Cross-table scanning was not run because the tables report different physical quantities in different units on partly different animals (Table 1 allocates distinct animals to the physiological, barrier and biochemical streams), so a cross-table match would be hard to interpret and the span model would be less reliable still. A within-table scan of Tables 4, 5 and 6 remains a reasonable further check that was not performed.

None are provided with the article, so the strongest available data-integrity check (raw-data duplication analysis) could not be attempted. Recorded as "not provided", which is distinct from "present but unreadable".

not_checked.location: Retraction notice and its stated grounds
not_checked.reason: The version of record is titled "RETRACTED ARTICLE" but the notice itself was not among the supplied files. The publisher's reasons are unknown to this review and no finding here is derived from or reconstructs them.

Read only via the whole-PDF statistical extraction, which found no test statistics anywhere in the document. Not examined line by line for citation or textual anomalies beyond the figure captions and load-bearing Results sentences reported above.

limitations: FIGURES WERE NOT READ. This agent reads text and tables and does not see figures; no figure extraction pass was run on this paper. That matters more than usual here: Figures 2, 5 and 8 are the sole source of the neuronal-injury, albumin-immunoreactivity and GFAP-immunoreactivity results, each of which supports a claim in the abstract, and none of those values appears in any table or in the body text. A substantial block of this paper's inferential claims was therefore not examined.

Every per-group sample size in this paper is given as a range ("6-8 rats at each point") rather than a value, so no test could be recomputed exactly. Each reconstruction used the end of the range most favourable to the authors' own claim -- n = 8 when testing a significance claim, n = 6 when testing a non-significance claim -- which means the reported discrepancies are conservative and would widen at the other end of the range.

The four unreachable-p results come from a targeted search of the roughly 500 asterisked comparisons in Tables 2-6, selected as the cells where a significance claim looked least supportable. They are a floor on the number of unsupportable asterisks in this paper, not a count of them.

Three of the four unreachable-p findings sit in Table 2, which was read from the publisher XML but not independently reconciled against the PDF in this stage. Stage 1 did reconcile Tables 3, 4 and 5 against PDF pages 6-8 and found the two sources agree exactly, including on the corrupted cells, which is good evidence that the XML extraction of this article is faithful; the Table 3 finding was itself PDF-reconciled and stands independently.

No GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE or DEBIT result appears in this review because every outcome variable in the paper is a continuous physiological or biochemical measure, which bars that family of checks by construction. No R cross-check was required, because no finding here reaches `impossible` -- an R engine was neither consulted nor needed.

This system reads one paper and reaches no external source. Two questions a reader needs in order to weigh the findings are outside its reach entirely: whether similar discrepancies appear in other papers by the same authors, and how the reported effect sizes compare with equivalent values from other studies in this area. Those parts of the interpretation are the reader's, not ours.

The multiplicity arithmetic could not be run at all, because every p-value in the paper is a threshold rather than a value. No count of claims lost to correction exists for this paper in either direction -- the absence of such a number is a fact about the reporting, not evidence that correction would leave the conclusions intact.

The tail-flick plausibility finding rests on an external benchmark from the thermal nociception literature (normal rat latencies of a few seconds; conventional cut-offs of about 10-15 s), not on anything the paper states. Under the rulebook it is capped at `suspicious`, is not the headline, and would be resolved by the authors simply stating their cut-off time.

tables_checked: Table 1 (Experimental Protocol in Nerve Lesion) -- 92 cells; all 18 row sums, 3 column sums and 2 grand-total reconciliations re-run at tolerance 0 in this stage; Al-group biochemical allocation summed separately

Table 2 (Physiological variables) -- 144 mean ± SD cells re-read at source; 5 comparisons reconstructed here (3 respiration, 1 body weight, 1 arterial pH); rectal-temperature and PaCO2 columns re-scanned for duplication with correctly-scoped spans

Table 3 (Von Frey / paw withdrawal / tail flick) -- all 54 cells re-read at source; 2 comparisons reconstructed here (paw withdrawal NL+Al 10 wk, Von Frey NL+Al 4 wk); reconciled against PDF page 6 in stage 1
Table 4 (BSCB breakdown and edema) -- 216 cells reviewed in stage 1 against PDF page 7; 3 corrupted cells identified

Table 5 (albumin, GFAP, MBP, HSP) -- 166 cells and the footnote re-read at source in this stage; 2 corrupted cells and 1 corrupted footnote confirmed; group structure checked against Table 1's allocation

questions_for_authors.question: Table 1 gives three different answers for the size of the study. input.report_markdown:
This is a rat study of chronic constriction nerve injury as a model of neuropathic pain. Three engineered metal nanoparticles (Ag, Cu, Al, 50-60 nm) are given intraperitoneally, and cerebrolysin -- a peptide preparation made by EverNeuroPharma, one of the study's listed funders -- is given intravenously. The paper reports that nerve lesion produces progressive hyperalgesia, blood-spinal cord barrier breakdown, cord edema, cytokine elevation and structural damage; that all three nanoparticles worsen all of it; and that cerebrolysin reverses all of it. The version of record is titled "RETRACTED ARTICLE". The retraction notice was not among the files supplied, so nothing below is derived from or reconstructs the publisher's grounds; every finding comes from the paper's own numbers.

## How this paper resists being checked

Almost every standard forensic check is inapplicable here, and that is worth stating before any finding, because the absence of such findings is not evidence the values are sound. The granularity family (GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE, DEBIT) works only on whole-number data; every outcome in this paper is a continuous physiological or biochemical measure, so those checks correctly refuse. Running the dispatcher over Table 3 typed all 54 cells successfully and then ran zero checks on them -- 0 of 54 -- for two independent structural reasons: continuous outcomes, and no cell carrying its own sample size. The same reasoning applies unchanged to Tables 2, 4, 5 and 6.

On top of that, the paper prints no test statistic, no degrees of freedom and no exact p-value anywhere in 25 pages. An automated extraction over the whole document recovered zero. Roughly five hundred comparisons are communicated entirely by asterisks. And the authors state in every table footnote that "for simplicity, the values are adjusted to nearest numbers" -- their descriptives are rounded to integers, which is a legitimate presentational choice that happens to destroy the precision a reader would need to reconstruct the tests.

The only route left is to work backwards from the group means and SDs. That is what was done.

## What the reconstruction showed

Twelve comparisons were reconstructed, chosen as the cells where a significance claim looked least supportable. Four could not be produced at all, and one comparison the paper calls non-significant turns out to be strongly significant. The direction matters: this is not a systematic bias toward more stars, which would be the signature of over-eager analysis. Errors run both ways, which is the signature of a table whose significance markers were not generated by the tests the paper describes.

Two details make these harder to explain away than they might look. First, every reconstruction used the sample size most favourable to the authors -- the top of the stated 6-8 range when testing a significance claim, the bottom when testing a claim of no difference. Second, the paper says it used ANOVA with Dunnett's correction, which is *more* conservative than the unadjusted two-group tests recomputed here. Both choices push in the authors' favour, and the discrepancies survive both.

A thirteenth comparison sits on the fence and is reported here rather than as a finding: Table 3's Von Frey weight for NL + Al NPs at 4 weeks (9 ± 5, unstarred) against a control of 15 ± 2 gives an achievable p-interval of [0.005, 0.082] at n = 6, which straddles 0.05. It cannot be adjudicated, and it is not counted against the paper.

## The arithmetic that does not depend on any test

Table 1 is the study's allocation table and it should be the easiest thing in the paper to verify: eighteen rows of whole animals. Six of seven sums fail at zero tolerance. What makes this more than a typo is the internal structure of the failures. Three row totals over-state by exactly two each; two column totals under-state by eight and six; and the printed grand total of 348 -- which matches the figure in the Methods text -- is arithmetically consistent only with the incorrect column totals, not with the animals actually listed. There is a consistent chain from the wrong intermediate figures to the headline N, and no chain from the actual data.

## What the paper collected but did not report

Table 1 sets aside 26 rats for biochemical analysis across the four aluminium-nanoparticle groups. Tables 5 and 6 -- the biochemical tables -- contain no aluminium rows at all; their captions cover only silver and copper. The abstract, having named all three metals, states that the ELISA proteins and cytokines were elevated "in nerve lesion that was exacerbated following NPs intoxication". For aluminium, no data in the paper supports that.

## Consistency, where it was found

It is worth saying what did reconcile. Fifteen of Table 1's eighteen per-group row totals add up exactly, and the Biochemical Analyses column reconciles exactly at 130. A duplication scan of Table 2's rectal-temperature and PaCO2 columns turned up exactly one identical pair among 306 comparisons, at a corrected coincidence probability of 0.034 -- weak, and materially weaker than the sweep's first estimate of 0.0001, which came from a span model fitted across variables that do not share a range. That correction is recorded because a duplication finding presented at the wrong strength is worse than none.

But this is thin. Most of the paper could not be checked, and among the small set of claims that could be, several do not hold.

## The bottom line

Four significance markers cannot be produced from the numbers printed beside them; one stated non-significance is contradicted by the same table at roughly twenty-five times the paper's own threshold; the study's sample size is stated three different ways by its own allocation table; five published values cannot be read as numbers; and the animal-level data that would settle all of it are not available. Two of the unsupportable asterisks sit on the primary pain outcome and on a claimed cerebrolysin benefit, which are the paper's central claims.

I have no confidence in the accuracy of the statistics reported in this study, and its conclusions should not be relied upon without the underlying per-animal data being made available for re-analysis.
